Sales reached $38M last year, but profitability has quietly eroded every year since 2016 despite genuinely differentiated, well-reviewed collections.
questions: What factors would you consider in building a profitability plan for Marigold Kids?
Sales per boutique have been falling even as the store base has grown. What might explain that, and where else could costs be leaking? Give me at least four ideas, grouped.
Calculate the revenue and gross profit a toy line could add per year if it performs like the comparable retailers, and compare that with the inventory and fixtures investment.
What would you recommend to the CEO, and what are the risks of adding toys to the boutiques?
key_data: Marigold Kids sells only in the U.S. today, with no international plans confirmed
The client has not set a specific profitability target — it wants the strongest defensible plan
Each seasonal collection is fully redesigned rather than iterated on, and the design and sourcing team has roughly doubled in headcount since 2016
Store count has grown from 140 to 220 boutiques since 2016, but average sales per boutique have declined over the same period
Leadership is weighing launching a new toy product line inside its existing boutiques, projected to require $4M in inventory and fixtures
Comparable apparel retailers that added a toy line saw it contribute 8-12% of store revenue within a year, typically at a lower gross margin than apparel
Marigold Kids' apparel gross margin today is 58%; a toy line at comparable retailers typically runs 35-40% gross margin

title: Help an EV Maker Break Into the B2B Fleet Market
prompt: Aeon Motors is a leading Japanese electric-vehicle maker with a dominant consumer position at home and abroad, but its B2B fleet sales — rental companies, corporations, government agencies — have stayed far below where its market share would suggest. The CEO wants a plan to fix it.
questions: What factors would you consider in building a plan for Aeon Motors to win fleet customers?
Why might fleet buyers be reluctant to choose Aeon even though consumers love the brand? Give me at least four ideas, grouped.
Calculate how many test drives the one-day event must convert in order to pay for itself.
What would you recommend the CEO do first, in what order, and what are the main risks?
key_data: Aeon Motors holds 60% of all Japanese battery-electric vehicles sold, almost entirely in the consumer segment
Japanese electric vehicles hold only 5% of the global EV market
The global EV market is projected to grow from roughly 4 million units this year to 35 million units within a decade
Aeon's fleet sales funnel runs prospect to quote request to test drive to signed contract; the prospect-to-test-drive conversion rate is well below the industry benchmark for fleet sales
Aeon is planning a one-day marketing event targeting 1,000 qualified fleet prospects to convert more of them to a test drive
The event is budgeted at $150,000, and each converted test drive is estimated to be worth $2,800 in expected fleet-contract value
Aeon's current model lineup includes only passenger cars — no vans, trucks, or buses, which make up a large share of typical fleet purchases

title: Reverse a Farm-Equipment Maker's Sales Decline in a Growing Market
prompt: Route & Furrow is a long-established U.S. farm-machinery brand. Even though the overall U.S. farm-tractor market grew last year, Route & Furrow's own tractor sales fell 15% to $650M. The CEO wants to know why the client is losing ground in a growing market, and how to reverse it.
questions: How would you structure the investigation into why Route & Furrow is losing ground in a growing market?
What could explain a falling sales number in a market that is growing? Give me at least four ideas, grouped into internal and external causes.
Calculate the break-even volume increase the company needs for the proposed price cut on its compact line to pay off.
What is your recommendation to the CEO to reverse the decline, and what are the main risks?
key_data: The overall U.S. farm tractor market actually grew 18% last year, driven by federal farm-aid payments and rising crop prices
The farm tractor market is fragmented: the top 5 manufacturers combined hold only 35% share
Route & Furrow sells three tractor classes: compact (under 40 HP), utility (40-100 HP), and high-horsepower (100+ HP)
Route & Furrow's compact-tractor line lost the most share of the three classes last year
A competitor's new entry-level compact tractor launched last year at a price 12% below Route & Furrow's comparable model
Route & Furrow is considering a 5% price cut on its compact line; each compact tractor currently sells for $28,000 with a $6,000 contribution margin, and the line sells 9,000 units a year

title: Grow Adoption of an Industrial IoT Monitoring Product
prompt: Coretemp Systems sells industrial air-conditioning units, maintenance services, and an IoT-enabled monitoring platform that watches a facility's cooling systems in real time and flags failures before they happen. Total revenue is $900M, but the monitoring software is a rounding error next to the hardware business. The CEO wants a real growth plan for the software specifically.
questions: How would you approach building a growth plan for Coretemp's monitoring software?

Facilities that have not adopted monitoring software cite uncertainty about return on investment. What could Coretemp do to remove that barrier and grow adoption? Give me at least four ideas, grouped.

Calculate the revenue the software would generate if Coretemp reached a larger share of the facilities that are not yet using any monitoring, and how that compares with the fixed cost of the platform.
What would you recommend to the CEO, and what are the risks to the plan?
key_data: The monitoring software works on cooling equipment from other manufacturers too, not just Coretemp's own units
Coretemp serves food processing, pharmaceutical production, and semiconductor fabrication facilities, among others
Of roughly 15,000 large manufacturing facilities in Coretemp's addressable market, only 3,500 currently use any monitoring software at all
The software is priced at $18,000 per facility per year
Building and supporting the software platform costs Coretemp a fixed $22M a year, regardless of how many facilities subscribe
A customer survey of non-adopters found the top cited reason was uncertainty about return on investment, not price or product fit
Facilities that use the monitoring software report a 20% reduction in unplanned downtime versus those that don't

title: Design a Growth Strategy for a Plateaued Kitchenware Retailer
prompt: Copper & Sage is a high-end kitchenware retailer — cookware, bakeware, small electrics — with 90 stores across the U.S. and Canada and a growing online channel, generating $190M a year. Growth has flattened over the last three years, and leadership wants a credible 3-year growth strategy.
questions: How would you approach building a three-year growth strategy for Copper & Sage?
What growth levers could a high-end kitchenware retailer pull beyond its current stores? Give me at least five ideas, grouped.
Calculate the annual profit contribution of a paid loyalty program per member, and the number of members needed to cover the one-time setup cost.
What is your recommendation on the loyalty program and the rest of the growth plan, and what could go wrong?
key_data: Online sales are about 8% of total revenue today
Copper & Sage sells to both individual consumers and business customers (boutique restaurants, upscale hotels)
The high-end segment of the North American kitchenware market is roughly $2B and growing slowly
Leadership is considering a paid loyalty program and ran a small third-party pilot last year
Pilot members spent $425 a year on average, versus $340 for the typical non-member customer
The loyalty program costs $40 per member per year to administer, and Copper & Sage's typical merchandise gross margin is 42%
Launching the program company-wide is projected to cost $3M in one-time setup, on top of the per-member running cost

title: Triple Revenue for a Direct-to-Consumer Fresh Dog Food Brand
prompt: Wildtail sells fresh, personalized dog food direct to consumers online, with $110M in sales last year. Its overall share of the total dog food market is under 1%, but within the direct-to-consumer segment specifically it holds 15% share. Growth is healthy, but leadership wants to triple revenue over the next three years and has asked for a plan.
questions: How would you approach Wildtail's goal of tripling revenue in three years?
What are the ways Wildtail could grow beyond its current direct-to-consumer base? Give me at least five ideas, grouped.
Calculate what the retail shelf deal would add in contribution, and how long it would take to recover the cost of the second production facility.
Would you recommend that Wildtail accept the retail deal? Give me your reasoning, the risks and the next steps.
key_data: The total U.S. dog food market is roughly $28B and growing modestly
The direct-to-consumer segment of dog food is small in absolute terms but growing far faster than the category overall
Two large incumbents control more than half of the total dog food market between them
Wildtail is weighing expansion into traditional retail (pet superstores, mass retailers) alongside its DTC channel
A major pet retailer has offered Wildtail a national shelf placement deal, but fulfilling it would require building a second production facility, costing $18M and required within a year of signing
The retail deal is projected to generate $9M in incremental annual revenue at a 30% contribution margin, versus DTC's own 55% contribution margin on existing sales

title: Reverse a Window Manufacturer's Market Share Slide
prompt: Solstice Window Co. is a vertically integrated window manufacturer — six factories, 25 service centers — that makes its own glass units, vinyl frames, and hardware. Sales grew steadily until last year, when the company started losing market share for the first time. Revenue was $140M last year. The CEO wants a plan to turn it around.
questions: What factors would you consider to understand why Solstice Window Co. is losing market share?
What could have caused a company that was growing steadily to start losing share? Give me at least four ideas, grouped.
Calculate how many units of the energy-efficient model the company needs to sell each year to break even on that product line.
What is your recommendation to the CEO on the smart-window idea and the rest of the turnaround, and what are the risks?
key_data: The U.S. window market is roughly $14B and fragmented across many regional and national players
Solstice sells to both individual homeowners and builders/contractors
Leadership is considering investing in a 'smart window' product line — automated tinting and voice-activated shades — to respond to the home-automation trend
The smart-window R&D investment is estimated at $12M over two years before any units can ship
An energy-efficient window model Solstice launched two years ago is still unprofitable at current volumes
That energy-efficient model sells for $420 per unit with a $110 contribution margin, against $85,000 in annual fixed costs allocated to the product line
Solstice's service centers currently handle installation and repair for its existing product lines only

title: Assess Entering a European Country's Chocolate Market
prompt: Cadence Confectionery is a European house of chocolate brands pursuing an active international expansion strategy. It's now weighing entry into a mid-sized Eastern European country with its best-selling chocolate bar and candy lines. The CEO wants your team to size the opportunity and make the call.
questions: What factors would Cadence Confectionery consider to decide whether to enter this country?
What are the main ways Cadence could enter, and what would be the pros and cons of each? Give me at least four ideas.
Calculate the gross profit Cadence could make at a given share of the chocolate market, and how long it takes to recover the entry investment.
What is your recommendation to the CEO, and what are the main market, financial and operational risks?
key_data: The country has a population of 8.5 million
Annual chocolate spending in the country is roughly $550M today, growing at 9% a year
Three multinational players together hold just over half the market; the rest is split among many small local producers
Cadence has no local manufacturing or distribution in the country today
Import tariffs would add roughly 12% to Cadence's landed cost versus a locally-produced competitor
Cadence's typical retail gross margin in markets it already operates in is 45%
Cadence would need a minimum of $15M in upfront marketing and distribution investment to enter credibly

title: Should a Mobile Virtual Network Operator Expand Into Energy Retail?
prompt: Nimbus Mobile is an Australian mobile virtual network operator — it buys wholesale capacity from a major carrier and resells phone plans under its own brand to 900,000 subscribers. Leadership is considering becoming a 'virtual' energy retailer too, reselling electricity and gas it doesn't generate itself, and hopes to hit $4M in profit within a year of launch. They want your read on whether that's realistic.
questions: What factors would you consider to judge whether Nimbus Mobile should become an energy retailer?
What advantages could Nimbus bring to energy retail, and what obstacles might it face? Give me at least four ideas on each side, grouped.
Calculate whether Nimbus can reach its profit goal in the first year, using the customers it could cross-sell, the margin per customer, the acquisition cost and the technology investment.
Do you think the profit goal is realistic? Give me your recommendation, the main risks and next steps.
key_data: Australia has roughly 10 million electricity customers and 5 million gas customers
The electricity retailing market is worth about $18B a year; gas retailing is worth about $3B a year; both grow 1-3% annually
Over 90 licensed electricity and gas retailers already compete in the market
Nimbus's cost to acquire a new energy customer, based on its mobile-business experience, runs about $85 per customer
A typical energy retail customer generates about $60 in annual margin for a virtual retailer with no generation assets
Nimbus believes it can cross-sell energy plans to 8% of its existing 900,000 mobile subscribers in year one, plus acquire a smaller number of entirely new customers through marketing
Nimbus's existing customer service and billing systems can support energy accounts with a one-time $6M technology investment

title: Should a Skincare Brand Expand Into Injectable Aesthetics?
prompt: Lumiere Dermaceuticals sells a well-known line of consumer skincare — creams, cleansers, masks. Leadership is considering branching into injectable aesthetics (botox-style treatments) distributed through plastic-surgeon and dermatology practices. They want your view on whether it's a sound move.
questions: What factors should Lumiere Dermaceuticals consider before moving into injectable aesthetics?
What would Lumiere need in order to succeed in a business that sells to medical practices instead of consumers? Give me at least four ideas, grouped.
Calculate how many treatment courses Lumiere would need to sell to reach its profit goal, and how that compares with a realistic share of the segment.
Would you recommend that Lumiere make the move? Give me your reasoning, the risks and the next steps.
key_data: Roughly 17 million cosmetic procedures are performed in the U.S. each year, growing 1-2% annually
The injectable segment specifically is dominated by two established players that together hold most of the segment
Lumiere's core skincare business sells direct-to-consumer through retail and its own site — it has no existing relationships with surgeon or dermatology practices
Entering this segment would require building an entirely new B2B sales force targeting practices, since Lumiere's current sales team only knows retail buyers
Lumiere wants to hit $10M in profit from the injectable line within a defined window
A typical injectable treatment course sells for $450 wholesale to the practice, with a 40% margin for the manufacturer
Lumiere estimates it could realistically capture only a single-digit share of the segment within its first few years, given two entrenched incumbents

title: Help a Food Bank Plan Its Regional Expansion
prompt: Harvest Alliance is one of the largest U.S. food banks. Donations surged during a recent economic downturn, and leadership wants to use that momentum to expand into new regions. This is a pro-bono engagement — help them think through where to expand and how much capacity they'll need.
questions: What factors would you consider to help Harvest Alliance decide where to expand?
What criteria could the food bank use to choose between regions? Give me at least four ideas, grouped.
Compare the two warehouse options and calculate which one is the cheaper way to get the capacity needed for the expansion.
What is your recommendation for the food bank's expansion, and what are the risks?
key_data: Donations jumped 55% last year to $155M, versus roughly $100M in a typical prior year
The share of households facing food insecurity varies widely by state, from under 10% to over 25%
Harvest Alliance wants at least 90% of all funds raised to go directly to hunger-relief programming, capping admin costs at 10%
The organization's single existing warehouse, which costs $1.5M a year to run, is now near its practical storage limit
Each $1 donated currently funds roughly 4 meals once packaging and distribution costs are netted out
Expanding into a new region is estimated to require warehouse capacity for 2 million pounds of food storage
A second, similarly-sized warehouse would cost $1.8M a year to lease and run; moving both locations' inventory into one larger warehouse instead would cost $2.9M a year all-in

title: Should an Electronics Maker Enter the Video-Game Market?
prompt: Vantable Electronics makes laptops, desktops, tablets, and phones for consumers, businesses, and government. With growth stalling across its core hardware lines, leadership is considering entering the U.S. video-game market — publishing mobile and PC games rather than hardware. They want your view on whether this makes sense.
questions: What factors should Vantable Electronics consider in deciding whether to enter the video-game market?
What could Vantable offer a game publisher that a typical new entrant lacks, and what would it be missing? Give me at least four ideas on each side.
Calculate whether the planned mobile game could pay back its development investment within the target window, given how many downloads it would need.
Would you recommend that Vantable enter the market? Give me your reasoning, the risks and the next steps.
key_data: The U.S. video-game market is worth about $40B and has been growing quickly
The market is fragmented across many publishers, with a handful of large names controlling a meaningful but not dominant share
Vantable wants to target the mass casual-gaming audience, not hardcore gamers
Vantable wants to pay back any investment within 2 years of a game's launch
Vantable is evaluating a $2M investment to develop and launch a mobile game
Comparable mass-market mobile games in this genre generate about $3.50 in lifetime net revenue per paying user, after platform fees
Industry benchmarks suggest roughly 4% of people who download a free mobile game convert into a paying user

title: Should a Children's Apparel Brand Enter the Toy Market?
prompt: Sundial Kids sells adventure-themed children's clothing through 180 of its own stores nationwide, with $950M in sales and a 4% margin. Leadership wants to grow sales 10% through a new product category and is considering entering the traditional toy market — specifically dolls — inside its existing stores. They want your assessment.
questions: What factors would you consider to decide whether Sundial Kids should enter the toy market?
What are the advantages and disadvantages of selling dolls only inside its own stores versus also placing them with mass retailers? Give me at least four ideas, grouped.
Calculate whether a doll line could get Sundial to the sales-growth target, and how much store space it would use.
What is your recommendation to leadership, and what are the main risks?
key_data: The U.S. toy market is large and fragmented, with no single player holding a dominant share
Sundial's existing 180 stores average $5.3M in annual sales each today
Sundial wants to hit the 10% sales growth target within a defined, reasonable window using this new line
A doll line would need dedicated shelf space in each store, estimated at 8% of existing floor space
Comparable apparel retailers that added a toy category saw it contribute 8-12% of total store revenue within a year
Sundial is deciding between selling dolls only in its own stores (DTC) versus also placing them in mass-market retailers
Mass-retailer placement would require a new wholesale sales function Sundial doesn't currently have, and typically comes with 15-20 points lower margin than direct retail

title: Should an Eyeglass Lens Maker Invest in Automated Production?
prompt: Clearview Optics is a mid-sized U.S. manufacturer of prescription eyeglass lenses, supplying major glasses retailers. Revenue fell 25% during a recent downturn as fewer people got eye exams and optical retailers temporarily closed. To improve its economics, Clearview is considering investing in a new digitized, automated production process. They want your advice on whether it makes sense.
questions: What factors would you consider in deciding whether Clearview Optics should invest in automated production?
What might Clearview gain and lose by automating? Give me at least four ideas on each side, grouped.
Calculate the annual cost savings from the new process, and how long the investment takes to pay back relative to the equipment's useful life.
What is your recommendation to the CEO, and what are the main risks of automating?
key_data: Roughly 75 million pairs of prescription eyeglasses are sold in the U.S. each year
Clearview sold 900,000 pairs of lenses last year at an average price of $48 per pair
The current manufacturing process has more than 10 discrete stages and is highly labor-intensive
The new automated process would consolidate and digitize most of these stages
Clearview's largest retail customer selects suppliers mainly on price, delivery speed, and defect rate — not brand
Current per-pair production cost is $31, and the new process is projected to bring that down to $24 per pair
The automation investment is estimated at $9M upfront, with a useful equipment life of 6 years

title: Compare Reshoring Automation vs. Moving Production Overseas for a Tire Maker
prompt: Ridgeline Tire Co. is a U.S. tire manufacturer whose sales fell 10% during a pandemic-driven drop in vehicle mileage, and management expects continued soft demand as remote work reduces driving. To protect margins, the CEO is weighing two cost-optimization options: moving production to a joint-venture factory in China, or investing in a more automated production line at its single existing Ohio plant. Which should they pursue?
questions: What factors would you consider when comparing the two cost-optimization options for Ridgeline Tire Co.?
What risks does each option carry beyond its cost savings? Give me at least four, grouped by option.
Calculate the annual savings of each option and how long each takes to pay back.
Which option would you recommend, and what could change your mind?
key_data: Ridgeline sells 80% of its tires in the U.S. and 20% internationally
Ridgeline sells both original-equipment tires (to carmakers) and replacement tires (to consumers)
Ridgeline operates only one production facility today, in Ohio, running near full capacity
The China joint-venture option requires a $60M upfront investment and is projected to cut per-tire production cost by 30%, but adds 6 weeks of shipping time to reach U.S. customers
The Ohio automation option requires a $35M upfront investment and is projected to cut per-tire production cost by 18%, with no change in shipping time
Ridgeline produces 12 million tires a year at an average production cost of $42 per tire today
Recent trade tensions have raised the possibility of new tariffs on tires imported from China, though none are currently in effect

title: Should a Point-of-Sale Software Company Move to the Cloud?
prompt: Ledger Point sells point-of-sale systems — hardware terminals plus on-premise software — to small restaurants and retailers, charging a one-time hardware fee plus an ongoing software fee. Cloud-based, subscription-only POS systems are rapidly gaining share industry-wide. Leadership is considering switching Ledger Point's own model entirely to the cloud. Should they?
questions: What factors would you consider in deciding whether Ledger Point should move to a cloud model?
What would change for Ledger Point's customers, costs and competitors if it switched? Give me at least four ideas, grouped.
Calculate the monthly subscription fee Ledger Point would need to charge to match its current revenue per customer over three years, and compare the migration cost with the savings.
Would you recommend the move? Give me your reasoning, the risks and the next steps.
key_data: The U.S. restaurant-and-retail POS software market is worth about $11B, and the cloud-based share of it is growing quickly
About 28% of restaurants and 20% of retailers currently use a cloud-based POS system
The POS software space is crowded with both long-established on-premise vendors and newer cloud-native entrants
Ledger Point currently charges a $1,200 one-time hardware/setup fee plus $40/month in software fees per customer location
Under the proposed cloud model, Ledger Point would drop the one-time fee and charge a single subscription fee only
Ledger Point wants the new subscription-only pricing to reach the same total revenue per customer over 3 years as the current model, to avoid a revenue hit during the transition
Moving to cloud is projected to cut Ledger Point's own hosting and support cost per customer by 35% starting in year 2, but requires a $14M platform-migration investment

title: Should a Fertilizer Producer Build New Capacity or Expand Its Existing Plant?
prompt: Bluestem AgriChem produces nitrogen, phosphate, and potash fertilizers at five U.S. factories, all currently running at capacity. With demand forecasts turning bullish, leadership wants to expand production and is deciding between building an entirely new factory or expanding one of its existing plants. The CEO wants your recommendation.
questions: What factors would you consider in deciding how Bluestem AgriChem should add capacity?
What are the advantages and disadvantages of a new factory versus expanding an existing plant? Give me at least four ideas, grouped.
Calculate the cost per ton of added capacity for each option, and say how the tax incentive for a new site could change the comparison.
Which option would you recommend, and what are the risks?
key_data: Bluestem currently produces 1.4 million tons of fertilizer annually across its five factories
U.S. fertilizer demand has grown a modest 1% a year over the past several years
There are roughly 80 operational fertilizer production sites in the U.S. today, and that number has been slowly increasing
The capacity expansion is budgeted at $450M in total
Either option — new factory or expansion — takes 2 years to design and 2 years to build before producing a single ton
State governments have offered tax incentives to offset part of the cost, given the jobs the project would create, but only for a brand-new facility, not an expansion of an existing site
A new factory would add 500,000 tons/year of capacity; expanding an existing plant would add 350,000 tons/year for the same total budget, since it can reuse existing infrastructure

title: Should a Clinic Chain Unify Onto a Single Scheduling Platform?
prompt: Meridian Health Clinics operates 450 primary-care clinics nationwide, built up through years of acquisitions. As a result, its clinics run a patchwork of different scheduling tools — some clinics still use spreadsheets. Leadership is considering purchasing a single, chain-wide patient-scheduling platform and wants it to pay for itself within a year. Is that realistic?
questions: What factors would you consider in deciding whether Meridian Health Clinics should adopt a single scheduling platform?
Where might the clinics gain value from the platform, and what could stand in the way? Give me at least four ideas, grouped.
Calculate whether the platform can pay for itself within a year, using the staff time recovered and the extra billable visits against its fees and implementation cost.
Is the one-year goal realistic? Give me your recommendation, the risks and the next steps.
key_data: Meridian is not specialized — its clinics offer general primary care, not a specific medical specialty
It's considered industry best practice to run one scheduling platform across an entire clinic chain rather than many disconnected tools
A single scheduling platform's fee for a chain this size runs $2,400 per clinic per year
The platform vendor projects each clinic recovers 3 hours of front-desk staff time per week through automated reminders and reduced no-shows
Meridian pays front-desk staff $22/hour on average
Reducing missed appointments is projected to add a meaningful number of billable visits per clinic per year, each worth $140 in average billed revenue to Meridian
The platform requires a $3.5M one-time, chain-wide implementation cost on top of the ongoing per-clinic fee

title: Should an Oncology Drug Get a New Cold-Chain Packaging Format?
prompt: Solace Pharma sells an oncology drug, distributed globally, that a small but meaningful share of patients find inconvenient and error-prone to store and dose correctly. After screening several options against strict requirements — cold storage, moisture and oxygen protection, dose control, tamper resistance — Solace has identified a new cold-chain packaging technology it could switch to. The CEO wants your recommendation on whether to make the switch.
questions: What factors would you consider in deciding whether Solace Pharma should switch to the new packaging?
How might better packaging affect patients, doctors and the business? Give me at least four ideas, grouped.
Calculate the added annual packaging cost, and how much the discontinuation rate would need to fall for the switch to pay off.
Would you recommend the switch? Give me your reasoning, the risks and the next steps.
key_data: Patients take multiple pills of this drug per day, alongside a couple of other supporting medications
Five other pharmaceutical companies offer competing drugs for this same cancer type
Solace holds roughly 2% of the global market for this drug category, or about 18,000 units sold per year
The drug's list price is $3,800 for a monthly supply
The patient population for this cancer type is not growing

The new packaging is projected to add $220 in cost per unit sold across all 18,000 units, but is expected to improve patient adherence enough to reduce treatment discontinuation by a meaningful margin
Every 1-point reduction in the discontinuation rate is estimated to be worth roughly 150 additional units sold per year, at Solace's existing 65% gross margin on the drug
